paragraphs.source_en: The Central Saharan pottery is the earliest pottery found so far in Africa (Fig. 4-1). At Tin Hanakaten in the Tassili the pottery has been present since the earliest Holocene occupation levels, dating at 9,420+200 BP (calBP 10,726±300) (Aumassip 2006). In the Acacus its presence is slightly later, dating to 8,950+55 BP (calBP 10,074±109) (Di Lernia & Garcea 2005). Although rather rare in these earliest levels, the pottery is one of the markers of general changes characteristic for the Epipalaeolithic period. With the climatic changes in the Early Holocene pottery appears alongside the microlithic industry, grinding stones and stone structures in the shelters, suggesting a more sedentary lifestyle than in the previous Late Pleistocene period. Pottery manufacture is just one end product of a series of cultural transformations (Rice 1999: 44).

paragraphs.source_en: The earliest Saharan pottery consists of sherds of broken vessels but no portable art so that this new technology seems to have been reserved for pots. Why did people need to make ceramic containers which could have been made of other materials, such as stone, wood, ostrich eggs or leather? Commonly accepted explanations of pottery origins and adoption are generally materialist, pots being considered as adaptive solutions to subsistence problems (Rice 1999).
